NAD(P) is a ligand, and binding it is a functional property that several unrelated SCOP folds and superfamilies have acquired. The most familiar case is the classic Rossmann-type dinucleotide-binding module, a beta-alpha-beta unit with a glycine-rich loop (GxGxxG-like) that cradles the pyrophosphate and the adenine ribose. This is the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domain in SCOP class c.2. Other NAD(P)-binding domains, such as the FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain in c.3, adopt different topologies, so the same cofactor is bound by distinct folds. The most defensible reading is that NAD(P) binding has arisen more than once, and that some of these occurrences are convergent, with no shared ancestry at the level that matters for function transfer.

Convergence is favored because the pyridine dinucleotide imposes strong chemical and geometric constraints. The pyrophosphate needs a positively charged helix N-terminus or loop, the adenine needs a hydrophobic pocket, and the nicotinamide needs a site near the catalytic residues for hydride transfer. Many different folds can supply these features, so similar binding geometry alone does not show a common origin. Divergence is evidenced by shared fold topology across the members of a superfamily, conserved sequence and structural motifs beyond the short dinucleotide motif, and conserved catalytic residues with consistent positions in the fold. Those signals support homology at superfamily or family level, and they are the appropriate basis for assigning SCOP superfamily and family membership.

Cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient for homology for these reasons. The GxGxxG-type motif is short and recurs across many proteins, so it produces false positives. Similar active-site geometry and catalytic chemistry can arise by convergence, as in other well-known cases of convergent catalytic sites. Ligand specificity can also change while the fold is conserved, for example NAD versus NADP selectivity, which is often governed by a residue at the end of the beta2 strand (acidic residues favor NAD, basic residues favor NADP), although this rule has exceptions. So a predicted NAD(P) binder should not inherit a specific function or enzyme class from a template without further support.

Limits and evidence needed: this answer uses pretrained model knowledge only, and no database search, structural alignment, or sequence profile was run. Confirming homology requires external evidence that was not checked here, namely structure-based comparison (e.g., DALI or TM-align scores with a significant Z-score), sequence profile or HMM searches with significant E-values, comparison of the full fold topology, and assessment of conserved catalytic residues and phylogenetic relationships. Template or representative selection should use the SCOP release-specific superfamily assignment, and the chosen representative should be checked for the conservation signals above rather than the cofactor motif alone. I have not verified specific SCOP identifiers beyond the class and superfamily labels cited here, so those should be confirmed against the SCOP release before use.
